Santa Maria Madre de Deus: A Hidden treasure

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Hidden treasure of immense archeological value lay undiscovered on the East London seabed for centuries until chanced upon by two local spear fishermen.

Unique Selling Point:
Two spear fishermen have stumbled on what appears to be a unique archaeological find off the East London Coast. Relics that could possibly belong to the Santa Maria Madre de Deus that went missing in 1643. This wreckage site has remained untouched and unexplored for 377 years. Carte Blanche gets an exclusive first look at this historical find.

Summary:
On 19 Sept 2019 while swimming back to shore after a dive, local spear fishermen Hennie Roos and Mathew Fenn encountered three cannon on the seabed off the Nahoon River Mouth, north-east of East London.

After the dive they contacted John Barry of Southern Cross Boating and Adrenalin, and a scuba dive on the site was arranged a week later which confirmed the presence of the cannon on the seabed. Subsequent dives have recorded further cannon on the site as well as anchors and pieces of dressed or cut stone that appear to be part of a ship’s ballast.

Based on the location of the site and the appearance of the guns it is suggested that the wreck may be that of the Portuguese naveta, Santa Maria Madre de Deus, believed to have been lost in the vicinity of Bonza Bay, in 1643, nine years before Van Riebeeck established the Dutch settlement in Table Bay.

A Dive team has been put together that will include the two spear fishermen, who will now learn to scuba dive and can become part of the retrieval endeavour.

Carte Blanche gets an exclusive first look at the site of the find and speaks to all the key players who will excavate the site over the next few months. We will take a boat trip and film the divers who will dive to see what more they can find and film some more fresh underwater footage of the cannons.

Further information:
The group of divers reported the find to Kevin Cole at the East London Museum and together they approached the South African Heritage Resources Agency (SAHRA, responsible for the management of South Africa’s underwater heritage resources). SAHRA was asked to consider the retrieval, under permit, of two of the cannon for display at the Museum and at the South Africa Coastal Education and Visitor Centre in the Nahoon Point Nature Reserve.

SAHRA’s Maritime and Underwater Cultural Heritage Unit responded in Oct 2019 indicating it was highly likely that the cannon were part of a shipwreck site and that an archaeologist would therefore have to be involved if any work on the site was to be considered.

Mr Cole therefore contacted John Gribble, maritime archaeologist at ACO Associates in Cape Town and a dive on the site by Mr Gribble in November 2019 confirmed that the site is almost certainly an unknown shipwreck.

Historical Portuguese wrecks on the South African coast:
At least thirteen Portuguese ships from ‘the Age of Exploration’, spanning approximately 200 years between the late 15th and 17th centuries, were wrecked along what is now the South African coast.

Since the early 1970s researchers, such as the late Graham Bell-Cross of the East London Museum, have worked to identify the location of the wrecks and together with discoveries by divers, most of the sites have now been located or the approximate place of their loss identified. Only the locations of the so-called “Soares” wreck (1505), possibly the earliest Portuguese loss in South African waters, and the Santa Maria Madre de Deus (1643) remain unconfirmed.

The Santa Maria Madre de Deus was a naveta, carrying at least 28 guns, and was lost on a return voyage from the East with a cargo of spice, Chinese porcelain and saltpetre, having departed Goa in early March 1643.

Bell-Cross suggested that there was a mid-17th century Portuguese wreck somewhere off Bonza Bay on the basis of porcelain shards, carnelian beads and other artefacts that have been collected near the mouth of the Qinira River in the past. The age and type of the wreck material found on the beach and the absence of any other known wreck from this period in the area led to the suggestion that this may be the wreck of the Santa Maria Madre de Deus.

The cannon recently discovered off the Nahoon River have the potential to finally give a name to this unnamed wreck, and possibly pin down the location of the Santa Maria Madre de Deus.

A site of potential national and international importance:
Portuguese and Spanish ships of the 15th and 16th centuries were the original vehicles of expansion into the East and New World respectively during the European Age of Exploration, but our knowledge of these vessels of exploration and trade is limited and based almost entirely on a small body of written records, drawings and paintings.

In the absence of documentary records, the only other source of primary information about Portuguese ships during this period is the wrecks of these ships. To date, relatively few Portuguese India-route shipwreck sites have been found, and almost all were subject to modern salvage by their finders before archaeologists had access to the sites.

Of the Portuguese wrecks previously found in South African waters, none have been subject to proper archaeological investigation. Interventions in these sites have tended to be salvage-driven with the focus on the recovery of saleable objects and artefacts with little interest in the wider site, its meaning or archaeological value.

As a possibly untouched 17th century Portuguese shipwreck, the Nahoon River Wreck is thus potentially very significant: both to our national underwater cultural heritage and in terms of what this wreck, if carefully, archaeologically investigated can add to the international body of knowledge about the ships of the Age of Exploration, the era which arguably kickstarted the process of globalisation which continues today.

Nahoon River Wreck Project:
A team comprising the finders of the wreck (Hennie Roos and Matt Fenn), Southern Cross Boating and Adrenalin (John Barry) and a number of East London divers has been formed to investigate the site. The project will be led by John Gribble, and the East London Museum has agreed to act as the conservation facility and artefact repository for the project.

John Gribble applied for and has been granted a permit by SAHRA for an initial pre-disturbance survey of the wreck, in an area covering the seabed between the Nahoon and Qinira Rivers. As part of the permit application process, descriptions, measurements and the positions of the cannons and other material already noted on the seabed have been lodged with and registered by SAHRA, to ensure the protection of these artefacts.

If the wreck proves to be that of the Santa Maria Madre de Deus, the initial non-intrusive recording and mapping of the site will be followed by the retrieval of cannon for museum display to mark the discovery and to add to the tangible, publicly accessible evidence of the rich maritime history of this part of our coast.

Following the pre-disturbance phase of the project, further, in depth investigation and possible excavation of the site is envisaged .

An important element of the current project is a public outreach and interaction programme to locate and record information about artefactual material collected from the beaches close to the wreck site, which may be related to the site. This is especially important in the light of the current increased incidences of ‘mini’ storm surge events. Anyone with wreck-related material from the Bonza Bay area, or with information about the location of such material on the beaches is encouraged to contact Kevin Cole or John Barry to allow the recording of this material which will form part of the project and wreck site archive and which may help towards our identification and understanding of the wreck.

The project will create an opportunity to promote maritime archaeology, especially the potential for collaboration in this field between archaeological professionals and members of the public.

The project will also be a valuable link to the promotion of the Nahoon precinct with its already established Nahoon Point Nature Reserve. It is also the area where the first human trace footprint and the East London Museum has been built in the shape of a foot. We can also get to see cannons and porcelainm from other shipwrecks that have been retrieved and are kept at the museum, which will give a better visual reference of what will be retrieved from the sea bed.

The area around the wreck is monitored by the coastal rangers from the nature reserve who report activity in the reserve and seaward of the high water tide line.

This wreck is legally protected under the terms of Section 35 of the National Heritage Resources Act (No. 25 of 1999) and that it may not be disturbed in any way, or anything removed from the site, except under a permit issued by SAHRA.

The existence of a 17th century Portuguese wreck on East London’s doorstep is something of potentially great heritage and tourism value to the city, and it is hoped that the work to investigate the site will contribute to the development of the historical narrative of the city, its past, and its future.

Press Release:


Two spearfishermen have made an astounding discovery off the East London coast, a shipwreck that could solve the mystery of the long-lost Santa Maria Madre de Deus that may have lain untouched and unexplored for almost four hundred years.

Script:


John Barry: Today is a slight breeze eight to nine knots and a slight swell, from yesterday's wind..
VO: Skipper John Barry, a master mariner with intimate knowledge of the majestic Eastern Cape shores is taking us on a voyage of discovery,// an exclusive first look at a newly found shipwreck site in East London just off the Nahoon River Mouth.
John Barry: It's one of those lucky days
// Beat with a whale…
VO: Such a lucky day we even had a whale sighting.

John Barry: You don't expect something to be lying right on your doorstep. For years, we've been walking on that beach just a few meters away and for at least 20 years of my life I've been looking for shipwrecks****

LINK: In September last year, two spearfishermen dived into the Indian Ocean off East London, hunting for fish.

Hennie: I normally come down to the beach most days just to see what the sea looks like before I plan a day and I bumped into Matt. I said let's go for a dive, it's looking quite good here.

VO: Hennie Roos and Matthew Fenn were about to make the find of a lifetime.

LINK: Nearly 400 years ago, a Portugese ship met its doom in these very same waters. And now, miraculously it seems, centuries later, their paths may have crossed.

Hennie: We speared some fish and on our way back,I dived onto some cannons and at first I thought it was a sewage pipe I called Matt over to have a look.

Matthew: I was surprised at first because I also thought it was a sewerage pipe.It is definitely a cannon which I've never seen anything like it.
Derek: Did everybody believe you at first?
Matthew: We tried to tell no one at first. We told John because he knows a lot more than we do about this.
John Barry: So they contacted me and I really didn't believe them. So we organised a scuba diver and we said to them we trust you, we believe you but we're gonna go look ourselves.We couldn't find the cannons initially that they found, we actually found others .
Derek: How did you feel that day?
John Barry: It's unbelievable all that history as a sailor to find, to go down and see that history lying down there, to try and imagine what happened.

VO: John knew exactly what to do - he went straight to Kevin Cole, Principle Natural Scientist at the East London Museum who understands the regulations around archeological finds.

Kevin: There's such a lot of heritage wealth locked up in our shipwrecks and to find a site that's potentially undisturbed and hasn't been impacted by treasure hunters is a rarity.

LINK: The days of the treasure hunters seem to be over. According to the permit to retrieve artefacts from the Nahoon wreck site, they have to be carefully protected and restored and the East London Museum has all the right facilities.

Kevin: There are hundreds of shipwrecks along our coast going back to the 15th century or even before.

VO: It was Kevin Cole's predecessor, the late Graham Bell-Cross, who documented many of the shipwrecks in the area and set a baseline for maritime studies at the museum.

Kevin: Graham had looked at survivor records for a ship believed to have been Santa Maria Madre De Deus, that went down in the Bonza Bay area. Lots of lives were lost, a number of survivors and artifacts that were brought to the museum, he could connect the puzzle and he put out the theory that a Portugese ship, possibly the Santa Maria went down in the Bonza Bay area in 1643.

LINK: At least 13 Portugese ships from the Age of Exploration, spanning about 200 years between the late 15th to 17th centuries have been shipwrecked along the South African coast.
VO: Two locations of wrecks remain a mystery, the “Soares” and the "Santa Maria Madre de Deus", a merchant ship that went missing on a return voyage from the East, with a cargo of spice, Chinese porcelain and saltpetre. It was carrying at least 28 guns.

Derek: What would tie up the cannon being found or other artifacts with the Santa Maria madre de deus?
Kevin: Porcelain for example, there's a great drawing that a previous maritime conservor Dion Smit did, when a lot of wood washed out in the Bonza Bay area. He couldn't pinpoint where the wreck site would have been but all these little bits, pieces of the puzzle have alluded to a shipwreck site.

VO: But in order for the puzzle to be put together fully and the potential wreck site explored, a maritime archeologist has been brought on board. John Gribble, now the project leader, holds the necessary permit from the Heritage Resources Agency.

Derek: When you first heard about this wreck, what were your thoughts?
John Gribble: Any new shipwreck turning up is always exciting and based on the photographs that I was sent of the cannon they'd seen on the seabed it looked like an early one, which is even more exciting.

VO: From around the 15th to 17th centuries, European trading vessels sailed around the Cape along the valuable East India trade routes, carrying luxuries like silk, spices, tea and porcelain... but it wasn’t always plain sailing.

Derek: Now these were primarily trade ships. Why did they need all the cannon?
John Gribble: It was a dangerous trip to the east. There were enemies along the way. In certain places they would have been pirates and other places they had competitors like theDutch who wanted to help themselves to the Portuguese trade and what the ships were carrying.

VO: Adding to their troubles, perilous seas and inclement weather patterns led many vessels astray along the Eastern Cape coastline. But the fate of the Santa Maria Madre de Deus remains a mystery. It is documented that three survivors were picked up near Mozambique by a passing ship, providing further clues as to the identity of the shipwreck.

John Gribble: And the story that they told was that they were off of the wreck with a captain, the captain's name tallies with the Madre de Deus. And that after the ship went down, they walked up to Mozambique.

VO: With John Gribble at the helm, this discovery has become a managed wreck site, curated by the East London Museum and Southern Cross Cruises with John Barry as project coordinator, leading the diving team.

LINK: This is a modern day treasure hunt. You can find it, but you can't take it with you right now. We're right above the dive site, the team is going down and they're going to try capture something for us. But only on camera.

VO: Matthew and Hennie are free diving alongside scuba divers Patrick Bertsch and Ivan Clarke,
John Barry: Where the site is close to shore and we haven't got good visibility. [00:05:27.20] Sometimes we have 2 meters, sometimes 3 meters.
Derek: What is the visibility today?
John Barry: It’s about 5 meters at the moment. So hopefully on the site it's not churned up.

VO: What makes this find potentially so important, is that most knowledge about the design of early Portuguese ships has been lost through the passage of time.

Derek: It has been described as a navetta. What is that?
John Gribble: What I've been able to figure out, is navetta was a relatively small ship. Quite a fast little ship, fewer decks than the bigger carex and the big trading ships that you always hear about when you read about Portuguese trade.

VO: for now, The team will receive basic training in maritime archeology with John Gribble, enabling them to gather information that might eventually point to the Santa Maria Madre de Deus.
John Barry: What we've done is Hennie and Matt have now started their scuba course.

VO: An hour has passed since the divers delved into these enigmatic waters and we're all holding our breath.

Derek: Hennie and Matthew, anything exciting to report
Matthew: Well we found the cannons and a ballast, looks like a ballast stone, big square very clean. it's definitely foreign and it's quite exciting to see.

Derek: Ivan I guess they do need the scuba guys here?
Ivan: When you get to spend time there, you really get to see there's so much more there that doesn't belong there, that's foreign covered in marine growth but definitely part of a shipwreck.

VO: On a calm day like this, the view was clearer, the divers saw hints of an anchor lying buried in sea moss. Further along Patrick spotted a brand new treasure, what appeared to be a broken piece of bronze.

Patrick: It looks like it’s from a cannon because it’s really massive and sticking in the sand. I could just see the greenish colour of the bronze.
Derek: So you're feeling quite confident that it is the Santa Maria Madre de dios
Ivan: if you ask me what I wanted to get out of this, I would have to answer, a positive ID. That would be great.
Derek: What would give you that positive ID?
Ivan: The one thing is to identify the cannon of being of portuguese origin. Another thing is every ship had a bell and every bell has a name. And if we could find that, that would be the ultimate.

John Gribble: The classic shipwreck thing is to find the ship's bell which often has the name on it although wrecks this early probably wouldn't, it was a much later thing.

VO: The team’s ultimate goal is a South African Heritage Resources Agency permit allowing them to remove the cannon(s) and other relics from the Ocean bed, and to add their find to the wealth of East London attractions.

Derek: What do you hope to get out of this?
Matthew: Not much. You can't take the find away. It's quite incredible I'm just keen to see where it goes in the future
Derek: So you may not fill the coffers but maybe your name will go down in history
Matthew: Definitely.

mihle@combinedartists.co.za 16 September 2020 Press Release: Two spearfishermen have made an astounding discovery off the East London coast, a shipwreck that could solve the mystery of the long-lost Santa Maria Madre de Deus that may have lain untouched and unexplored for almost four hundred years. Script: John Barry: Today is a slight breeze eight to nine knots and a slight swell, from yesterday's wind.. VO: Skipper John Barry, a master mariner with intimate knowledge of the majestic Eastern Cape shores is taking us on a voyage of discovery,// an exclusive first look at a newly found shipwreck site in East London just off the Nahoon River Mouth. John Barry: It's one of those lucky days // Beat with a whale… VO: Such a lucky day we even had a whale sighting. John Barry: You don't expect something to be lying right on your doorstep. For years, we've been walking on that beach just a few meters away and for at least 20 years of my life I've been looking for shipwrecks**** LINK: In September last year, two spearfishermen dived into the Indian Ocean off East London, hunting for fish. Hennie: I normally come down to the beach most days just to see what the sea looks like before I plan a day and I bumped into Matt. I said let's go for a dive, it's looking quite good here. VO: Hennie Roos and Matthew Fenn were about to make the find of a lifetime. LINK: Nearly 400 years ago, a Portugese ship met its doom in these very same waters. And now, miraculously it seems, centuries later, their paths may have crossed. Hennie: We speared some fish and on our way back,I dived onto some cannons and at first I thought it was a sewage pipe I called Matt over to have a look. Matthew: I was surprised at first because I also thought it was a sewerage pipe.It is definitely a cannon which I've never seen anything like it. Derek: Did everybody believe you at first? Matthew: We tried to tell no one at first. We told John because he knows a lot more than we do about this. John Barry: So they contacted me and I really didn't believe them. So we organised a scuba diver and we said to them we trust you, we believe you but we're gonna go look ourselves.We couldn't find the cannons initially that they found, we actually found others . Derek: How did you feel that day? John Barry: It's unbelievable all that history as a sailor to find, to go down and see that history lying down there, to try and imagine what happened. VO: John knew exactly what to do - he went straight to Kevin Cole, Principle Natural Scientist at the East London Museum who understands the regulations around archeological finds. Kevin: There's such a lot of heritage wealth locked up in our shipwrecks and to find a site that's potentially undisturbed and hasn't been impacted by treasure hunters is a rarity. LINK: The days of the treasure hunters seem to be over. According to the permit to retrieve artefacts from the Nahoon wreck site, they have to be carefully protected and restored and the East London Museum has all the right facilities. Kevin: There are hundreds of shipwrecks along our coast going back to the 15th century or even before. VO: It was Kevin Cole's predecessor, the late Graham Bell-Cross, who documented many of the shipwrecks in the area and set a baseline for maritime studies at the museum. Kevin: Graham had looked at survivor records for a ship believed to have been Santa Maria Madre De Deus, that went down in the Bonza Bay area. Lots of lives were lost, a number of survivors and artifacts that were brought to the museum, he could connect the puzzle and he put out the theory that a Portugese ship, possibly the Santa Maria went down in the Bonza Bay area in 1643. LINK: At least 13 Portugese ships from the Age of Exploration, spanning about 200 years between the late 15th to 17th centuries have been shipwrecked along the South African coast. VO: Two locations of wrecks remain a mystery, the “Soares” and the "Santa Maria Madre de Deus", a merchant ship that went missing on a return voyage from the East, with a cargo of spice, Chinese porcelain and saltpetre. It was carrying at least 28 guns. Derek: What would tie up the cannon being found or other artifacts with the Santa Maria madre de deus? Kevin: Porcelain for example, there's a great drawing that a previous maritime conservor Dion Smit did, when a lot of wood washed out in the Bonza Bay area. He couldn't pinpoint where the wreck site would have been but all these little bits, pieces of the puzzle have alluded to a shipwreck site. VO: But in order for the puzzle to be put together fully and the potential wreck site explored, a maritime archeologist has been brought on board. John Gribble, now the project leader, holds the necessary permit from the Heritage Resources Agency. Derek: When you first heard about this wreck, what were your thoughts? John Gribble: Any new shipwreck turning up is always exciting and based on the photographs that I was sent of the cannon they'd seen on the seabed it looked like an early one, which is even more exciting. VO: From around the 15th to 17th centuries, European trading vessels sailed around the Cape along the valuable East India trade routes, carrying luxuries like silk, spices, tea and porcelain... but it wasn’t always plain sailing. Derek: Now these were primarily trade ships. Why did they need all the cannon? John Gribble: It was a dangerous trip to the east. There were enemies along the way. In certain places they would have been pirates and other places they had competitors like theDutch who wanted to help themselves to the Portuguese trade and what the ships were carrying. VO: Adding to their troubles, perilous seas and inclement weather patterns led many vessels astray along the Eastern Cape coastline. But the fate of the Santa Maria Madre de Deus remains a mystery. It is documented that three survivors were picked up near Mozambique by a passing ship, providing further clues as to the identity of the shipwreck. John Gribble: And the story that they told was that they were off of the wreck with a captain, the captain's name tallies with the Madre de Deus. And that after the ship went down, they walked up to Mozambique. VO: With John Gribble at the helm, this discovery has become a managed wreck site, curated by the East London Museum and Southern Cross Cruises with John Barry as project coordinator, leading the diving team. LINK: This is a modern day treasure hunt. You can find it, but you can't take it with you right now. We're right above the dive site, the team is going down and they're going to try capture something for us. But only on camera. VO: Matthew and Hennie are free diving alongside scuba divers Patrick Bertsch and Ivan Clarke, John Barry: Where the site is close to shore and we haven't got good visibility. [00:05:27.20] Sometimes we have 2 meters, sometimes 3 meters. Derek: What is the visibility today? John Barry: It’s about 5 meters at the moment. So hopefully on the site it's not churned up. VO: What makes this find potentially so important, is that most knowledge about the design of early Portuguese ships has been lost through the passage of time. Derek: It has been described as a navetta. What is that? John Gribble: What I've been able to figure out, is navetta was a relatively small ship. Quite a fast little ship, fewer decks than the bigger carex and the big trading ships that you always hear about when you read about Portuguese trade. VO: for now, The team will receive basic training in maritime archeology with John Gribble, enabling them to gather information that might eventually point to the Santa Maria Madre de Deus. John Barry: What we've done is Hennie and Matt have now started their scuba course. VO: An hour has passed since the divers delved into these enigmatic waters and we're all holding our breath. Derek: Hennie and Matthew, anything exciting to report Matthew: Well we found the cannons and a ballast, looks like a ballast stone, big square very clean. it's definitely foreign and it's quite exciting to see. Derek: Ivan I guess they do need the scuba guys here? Ivan: When you get to spend time there, you really get to see there's so much more there that doesn't belong there, that's foreign covered in marine growth but definitely part of a shipwreck. VO: On a calm day like this, the view was clearer, the divers saw hints of an anchor lying buried in sea moss. Further along Patrick spotted a brand new treasure, what appeared to be a broken piece of bronze. Patrick: It looks like it’s from a cannon because it’s really massive and sticking in the sand. I could just see the greenish colour of the bronze. Derek: So you're feeling quite confident that it is the Santa Maria Madre de dios Ivan: if you ask me what I wanted to get out of this, I would have to answer, a positive ID. That would be great. Derek: What would give you that positive ID? Ivan: The one thing is to identify the cannon of being of portuguese origin. Another thing is every ship had a bell and every bell has a name. And if we could find that, that would be the ultimate. John Gribble: The classic shipwreck thing is to find the ship's bell which often has the name on it although wrecks this early probably wouldn't, it was a much later thing. VO: The team’s ultimate goal is a South African Heritage Resources Agency permit allowing them to remove the cannon(s) and other relics from the Ocean bed, and to add their find to the wealth of East London attractions. Derek: What do you hope to get out of this? Matthew: Not much. You can't take the find away. It's quite incredible I'm just keen to see where it goes in the future Derek: So you may not fill the coffers but maybe your name will go down in history Matthew: Definitely.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Hidden treasure of immense archeological value lay undiscovered on the East London seabed for centuries until chanced upon by two local spear fishermen.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Two spear fishermen have stumbled on what appears to be a unique archaeological find off the East London Coast. Relics that could possibly belong to the Santa Maria Madre de Deus that went missing in 1643. This wreckage site has remained untouched and unexplored for 377 years. Carte Blanche gets an exclusive first look at this historical find.
metadata.Summary: On 19 Sept 2019 while swimming back to shore after a dive, local spear fishermen Hennie Roos and Mathew Fenn encountered three cannon on the seabed off the Nahoon River Mouth, north-east of East London. After the dive they contacted John Barry of Southern Cross Boating and Adrenalin, and a scuba dive on the site was arranged a week later which confirmed the presence of the cannon on the seabed. Subsequent dives have recorded further cannon on the site as well as anchors and pieces of dressed or cut stone that appear to be part of a ship’s ballast. Based on the location of the site and the appearance of the guns it is suggested that the wreck may be that of the Portuguese naveta, Santa Maria Madre de Deus, believed to have been lost in the vicinity of Bonza Bay, in 1643, nine years before Van Riebeeck established the Dutch settlement in Table Bay. A Dive team has been put together that will include the two spear fishermen, who will now learn to scuba dive and can become part of the retrieval endeavour. Carte Blanche gets an exclusive first look at the site of the find and speaks to all the key players who will excavate the site over the next few months. We will take a boat trip and film the divers who will dive to see what more they can find and film some more fresh underwater footage of the cannons.
metadata.Further information: The group of divers reported the find to Kevin Cole at the East London Museum and together they approached the South African Heritage Resources Agency (SAHRA, responsible for the management of South Africa’s underwater heritage resources). SAHRA was asked to consider the retrieval, under permit, of two of the cannon for display at the Museum and at the South Africa Coastal Education and Visitor Centre in the Nahoon Point Nature Reserve. SAHRA’s Maritime and Underwater Cultural Heritage Unit responded in Oct 2019 indicating it was highly likely that the cannon were part of a shipwreck site and that an archaeologist would therefore have to be involved if any work on the site was to be considered. Mr Cole therefore contacted John Gribble, maritime archaeologist at ACO Associates in Cape Town and a dive on the site by Mr Gribble in November 2019 confirmed that the site is almost certainly an unknown shipwreck. Historical Portuguese wrecks on the South African coast: At least thirteen Portuguese ships from ‘the Age of Exploration’, spanning approximately 200 years between the late 15th and 17th centuries, were wrecked along what is now the South African coast. Since the early 1970s researchers, such as the late Graham Bell-Cross of the East London Museum, have worked to identify the location of the wrecks and together with discoveries by divers, most of the sites have now been located or the approximate place of their loss identified. Only the locations of the so-called “Soares” wreck (1505), possibly the earliest Portuguese loss in South African waters, and the Santa Maria Madre de Deus (1643) remain unconfirmed. The Santa Maria Madre de Deus was a naveta, carrying at least 28 guns, and was lost on a return voyage from the East with a cargo of spice, Chinese porcelain and saltpetre, having departed Goa in early March 1643. Bell-Cross suggested that there was a mid-17th century Portuguese wreck somewhere off Bonza Bay on the basis of porcelain shards, carnelian beads and other artefacts that have been collected near the mouth of the Qinira River in the past. The age and type of the wreck material found on the beach and the absence of any other known wreck from this period in the area led to the suggestion that this may be the wreck of the Santa Maria Madre de Deus. The cannon recently discovered off the Nahoon River have the potential to finally give a name to this unnamed wreck, and possibly pin down the location of the Santa Maria Madre de Deus. A site of potential national and international importance: Portuguese and Spanish ships of the 15th and 16th centuries were the original vehicles of expansion into the East and New World respectively during the European Age of Exploration, but our knowledge of these vessels of exploration and trade is limited and based almost entirely on a small body of written records, drawings and paintings. In the absence of documentary records, the only other source of primary information about Portuguese ships during this period is the wrecks of these ships. To date, relatively few Portuguese India-route shipwreck sites have been found, and almost all were subject to modern salvage by their finders before archaeologists had access to the sites. Of the Portuguese wrecks previously found in South African waters, none have been subject to proper archaeological investigation. Interventions in these sites have tended to be salvage-driven with the focus on the recovery of saleable objects and artefacts with little interest in the wider site, its meaning or archaeological value. As a possibly untouched 17th century Portuguese shipwreck, the Nahoon River Wreck is thus potentially very significant: both to our national underwater cultural heritage and in terms of what this wreck, if carefully, archaeologically investigated can add to the international body of knowledge about the ships of the Age of Exploration, the era which arguably kickstarted the process of globalisation which continues today. Nahoon River Wreck Project: A team comprising the finders of the wreck (Hennie Roos and Matt Fenn), Southern Cross Boating and Adrenalin (John Barry) and a number of East London divers has been formed to investigate the site. The project will be led by John Gribble, and the East London Museum has agreed to act as the conservation facility and artefact repository for the project. John Gribble applied for and has been granted a permit by SAHRA for an initial pre-disturbance survey of the wreck, in an area covering the seabed between the Nahoon and Qinira Rivers. As part of the permit application process, descriptions, measurements and the positions of the cannons and other material already noted on the seabed have been lodged with and registered by SAHRA, to ensure the protection of these artefacts. If the wreck proves to be that of the Santa Maria Madre de Deus, the initial non-intrusive recording and mapping of the site will be followed by the retrieval of cannon for museum display to mark the discovery and to add to the tangible, publicly accessible evidence of the rich maritime history of this part of our coast. Following the pre-disturbance phase of the project, further, in depth investigation and possible excavation of the site is envisaged . An important element of the current project is a public outreach and interaction programme to locate and record information about artefactual material collected from the beaches close to the wreck site, which may be related to the site. This is especially important in the light of the current increased incidences of ‘mini’ storm surge events. Anyone with wreck-related material from the Bonza Bay area, or with information about the location of such material on the beaches is encouraged to contact Kevin Cole or John Barry to allow the recording of this material which will form part of the project and wreck site archive and which may help towards our identification and understanding of the wreck. The project will create an opportunity to promote maritime archaeology, especially the potential for collaboration in this field between archaeological professionals and members of the public. The project will also be a valuable link to the promotion of the Nahoon precinct with its already established Nahoon Point Nature Reserve. It is also the area where the first human trace footprint and the East London Museum has been built in the shape of a foot. We can also get to see cannons and porcelainm from other shipwrecks that have been retrieved and are kept at the museum, which will give a better visual reference of what will be retrieved from the sea bed. The area around the wreck is monitored by the coastal rangers from the nature reserve who report activity in the reserve and seaward of the high water tide line. This wreck is legally protected under the terms of Section 35 of the National Heritage Resources Act (No. 25 of 1999) and that it may not be disturbed in any way, or anything removed from the site, except under a permit issued by SAHRA. The existence of a 17th century Portuguese wreck on East London’s doorstep is something of potentially great heritage and tourism value to the city, and it is hoped that the work to investigate the site will contribute to the development of the historical narrative of the city, its past, and its future.
